title: Developmental Disorders
summary: Pervasive developmental disorders such as autism, intellectual disability (formerly mental retardation) with its levels and causes, related disorders, and learning disorders like dyslexia.

lesson.title: When development takes a different path
lesson.hook: A two-year-old does not answer to his name, never points at things he wants, and lines up his toy cars in perfect rows for hours. His grandmother says he is just stubborn. A specialist suspects something else.

slides.heading: What developmental disorders affect
slides.body:
The essential feature of **developmental disorders** is a problem in acquiring **cognitive, language, motor or social skills**. Many are **chronic**, persisting into adulthood, though in mild cases good **adaptation** or even recovery can occur.

**Pervasive developmental disorders** affect **social adjustment** and many areas at once. Others, such as **intellectual disability** and **learning disorders**, impair cognition without necessarily affecting social adjustment.

slides.heading: Why 'pervasive'?
slides.body:
In DSM-IV, four conditions made up the **pervasive developmental disorders**: **autism**, **Asperger's disorder**, **Rett's disorder** and **childhood disintegrative disorder**. They were seen as the most **devastating and perplexing** childhood disorders.

'Pervasive' means problems spread across **language, attention, social responsiveness, perception and motor development**, so children often need **special educational settings**. DSM-5 later grouped most of these as **autism spectrum disorder**.

slides.heading: Autism
slides.body:
**Autism** was first identified as a distinct syndrome by American psychiatrist **Leo Kanner** in **1943**. Symptoms appear **before age 3**, often in infancy. Children are typically very **unresponsive** to others, **uncommunicative**, **repetitive** and **rigid**.

About **80%** are **boys**. DSM-IV-era sources gave about **5 in 10,000**; with wider definitions, the WHO now estimates about **1 in 100** children are autistic.

terms.meaning: Little interest in people; no cuddling, poor eye contact, may dislike affection
Repeating exactly what was just heard, immediately or later (delayed echolalia)
Saying 'you' for 'I', for example 'You want juice'
Repetitive behaviour, limited pretend play, distress at changes in routine

slides.question: A child who repeats the exact sentence he has just heard is showing:
slides.why: Echolalia is repeating speech; echopraxia is repeating actions.

slides.heading: Causes: from blame to biology
slides.body:
Early psychodynamic and behavioural theorists, notably **Bettelheim (1967)**, blamed cold, distant '**refrigerator mothers**'. This idea has been **thoroughly rejected**: parenting style does not cause autism.

Research now points to **biological** and **cognitive** causes: strong **genetic** influence, more **seizures** than other children, and abnormal **neurotransmission** that disrupts communication between neurons. Vaccines have been extensively studied and do **not** cause autism.

slides.question: The 'refrigerator mother' theory of autism is now:
options: Rejected; autism has mainly biological causes
slides.why: Parenting style does not cause autism; genetic and neurological factors are central.

slides.heading: Outlook and treatment
slides.body:
A significant proportion of autistic children also have **intellectual disability**. Older studies reported that up to **90%** remained severely disabled as adults; the highest-functioning adults still face difficulties with **social interaction, communication** and **restricted interests**.

No treatment reverses autism, but **behavioural therapy**, **communication training**, **parent training** and **community integration** help children adapt. **Medication** treats specific symptoms for limited periods, not the whole syndrome.

slides.heading: Daniel's routine
slides.story: Three-year-old Daniel in Port Harcourt rarely looks at his mother, answers 'Do you want rice?' with 'You want rice', and screams if his cup is a different colour. Relatives blame his mother for being 'too busy'. A paediatric team explains this is autism, not bad parenting, and starts speech and behavioural therapy.
slides.takeaway: Autism shows in social, language and behavioural patterns, and is not caused by parenting style.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'briefly discuss autism as a pervasive developmental disorder'. Include Kanner (1943), onset before 3, the triad of social, communication and repetitive problems, sex ratio, causes and treatment. Mention the refrigerator-mother theory only to show it was rejected. Trap: confusing echolalia (words) with echopraxia (actions).
slides.sampleQuestion: Autism was first identified as a distinct syndrome by: (a) Bettelheim (1967) (b) Kanner (1943) (c) Asperger (1980) (d) Freud (1900)
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (b). In essays, note that Bettelheim's refrigerator-mother idea has been discredited and that causes are mainly biological.

points: Developmental disorders affect cognitive, language, motor or social skills.
Pervasive disorders affect many domains, including social adjustment.
Autism: Kanner (1943), onset before 3, mostly boys.
Signs: aloofness, echolalia, pronoun reversal, rigidity.
Causes are biological, not cold parenting; therapy helps adaptation.

lesson.title: Defining intellectual disability
lesson.hook: A 15-year-old has an IQ of 65 but runs his family's provision shop, gives correct change and greets every customer by name. Does he have an intellectual disability? The answer needs more than an IQ score.

slides.heading: Definition
slides.body:
**Intellectual disability**, called **mental retardation** in older sources, means substantial limitations in present functioning (AAMR). It requires **significantly below-average intellectual functioning** (IQ about **70 or below**), **plus** limitations in **two or more adaptive skill areas**, beginning **before age 18**.

Today the less stigmatising terms **developmental disability** and **intellectual disability** are preferred (Phares, 2003).

terms.meaning: Talking, understanding and relating to others
Dressing, washing, cooking, managing a home
Using transport, shops and services; making choices
Practical reading and maths, free time and employment

slides.question: A diagnosis of intellectual disability requires low intellectual functioning plus:
options: Limitations in at least two adaptive skill areas, starting before 18
slides.why: IQ alone is not enough; adaptive limitations beginning before 18 are required.

slides.heading: Prevalence and controversy
slides.body:
About **1%** of people receive this diagnosis (APA, 2000), around **three-fifths** of them **male**, and the vast majority are **mildly** affected.

It is **controversial** and **difficult to diagnose**, partly because of **stereotypes**, and mainly because it rests on **intelligence**, which is hard to define (Gould, 1981; Kamin, 1974). It often occurs alongside **autism**.

slides.heading: Characteristics
slides.body:
The most consistent sign is **learning very slowly**. Other common difficulties involve **attention**, **short-term memory**, **planning** and **language**.

These limitations tend to be more marked in people who have lived in **institutions**, which offer fewer learning opportunities.

steps.title: Mild (IQ 50 to 70)
steps.detail: About 85%; 'educable'; can benefit from school and support themselves, with help under stress.

steps.title: Moderate (IQ 35 to 49)
steps.detail: About 10%; can learn self-care and do supervised unskilled or semi-skilled work.

steps.title: Severe (IQ 20 to 34)
steps.detail: Poor motor development and little speech before 5; may learn basic hygiene and simple supervised tasks.

steps.title: Profound (below 20)
steps.detail: Severe limits in adaptive and motor skills; often physical problems; need constant care.

slides.heading: Mild intellectual disability
slides.body:
**Mild** cases are usually not recognised until a child **starts school** and is assessed. Performance often **improves with age**, and some people shed the label after school, working in **skilled or semi-skilled** jobs.

Mild cases are linked mainly to **socio-cultural and psychological** causes: **poor, unstimulating environments**, weak **parent-child interaction**, and **few early learning experiences**. Biological factors, such as a mother's **drinking, drug use** or **malnutrition** in pregnancy, also play a part.

slides.question: Mild intellectual disability is usually first recognised:
options: When the child starts school and is assessed
slides.why: Mild cases often go unnoticed until school demands reveal slow learning.

slides.heading: Bisi's progress
slides.story: Bisi struggled in primary school and was assessed with mild intellectual disability. With patient teaching, practical maths and vocational training, she learned tailoring. At 25 she runs a small sewing business, though she calls her aunt when a big order stresses her. Her community simply knows her as a good tailor.
slides.takeaway: People with mild intellectual disability can benefit from schooling and support themselves, with help under stress.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect matching: a description to mild, moderate, severe or profound. Learn the IQ ranges and percentages (85% mild, 10% moderate). Definitions must include both low IQ and adaptive limits, with onset before 18. Trap: diagnosing from IQ alone. Use 'intellectual disability' in your own writing while recognising the older term.
slides.sampleQuestion: About 85% of people with intellectual disability fall into which level? (a) mild (b) moderate (c) severe (d) profound
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (a), IQ 50 to 70. Describe what they can achieve: schooling and self-support, with help under stress.

points: Intellectual disability: IQ about 70 or below plus adaptive limits, before 18.
About 1% are diagnosed, around three-fifths male, mostly mild.
Hard to diagnose because intelligence is hard to define.
Levels: mild (85%), moderate (10%), severe, profound.
Mild cases link mainly to poor environments, plus some prenatal factors.

questions.explanation: Slow learning is the most consistent feature.

questions.explanation: Onset must be before 18.

questions.explanation: Defining intelligence and overcoming stereotypes are core difficulties.

questions.explanation: About 10% function at the moderate level.

Only if a parent requests it
questions.explanation: Diagnosis needs both low IQ and adaptive limitations.

questions.explanation: IQ 35 to 49 with self-care and supervised work fits moderate.

questions.stem: A five-year-old has almost no speech and poor motor development, and later learns basic hygiene at a special school. This fits:
questions.explanation: Little speech and poor motor skills before 5, with basic hygiene learned later, describe severe disability.

questions.stem: Mild intellectual disability is linked mainly to:
options: Socio-cultural and psychological factors such as poor, unstimulating environments
questions.explanation: Mild cases are associated mainly with environmental deprivation, plus some biological factors.

questions.stem: Which statement about mild intellectual disability is correct?
options: It is usually recognised at birth
It is often not recognised until school, and performance may improve with age
questions.explanation: Mild cases emerge in school and often improve.

questions.stem: All of the following are adaptive skill areas EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Eye colour is not an adaptive skill.

questions.stem: I. About 85% of cases are mild. II. Diagnosis can rest on IQ alone. III. Around three-fifths of those diagnosed are male. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. Adaptive limitations are also required.

questions.stem: Why are limitations often more marked in people who lived in institutions?
options: Institutional settings often offer fewer learning and social opportunities
questions.explanation: Limited stimulation in institutions can worsen attention, memory and language difficulties.

questions.stem: Why have terms like 'intellectual disability' replaced 'mental retardation'?
options: It is now a physical illness
questions.explanation: Less stigmatising language is preferred in clinical and educational settings.

lesson.title: Genes, pregnancy and environment
lesson.hook: One child has an extra chromosome from the moment of conception. Another was born healthy but went months without enough food. Both may develop intellectual disability. Why is it called a symptom, not a disease?

slides.heading: A symptom with many causes
slides.body: Intellectual disability is a **symptom**, not one disease, with **many causes**: **chromosomal disorders**, **prenatal** exposure to drugs or **infections**, complications at **birth**, **brain trauma** after birth, **metabolic or nutritional** problems, **brain disease**, and **psychosocial disadvantage** such as deprivation, abuse and neglect.

slides.heading: Down syndrome
slides.body:
**Down syndrome**, or **trisomy 21**, is a chromosomal disorder. Cells have **47 chromosomes** instead of 46, because of an **extra chromosome 21**. The most common form is **not inherited**: it arises at **conception**, and its likelihood rises with the mother's **age**.

Children typically have a recognisable facial appearance, including upward-slanting eyes, and often **heart malformations**.

slides.heading: Fragile X and PKU
slides.body:
**Fragile X syndrome** is a single-gene condition: a gene near the tip of the **X chromosome** (FMR1) is altered, making that site appear '**fragile**'. It can cause intellectual disability, **autistic-like** behaviour and speech problems. Affected males often have **large ears** and a **long face**.

**Phenylketonuria (PKU)** is a **metabolic** disorder in which the body cannot break down phenylalanine. Caught early by newborn screening, a **special diet** prevents disability.

slides.question: Down syndrome is caused by:
options: A single gene on the X chromosome
slides.why: Trisomy 21 means an extra copy of chromosome 21, giving 47 chromosomes.

slides.heading: Detecting chromosomal problems
slides.body:
Chromosomal problems can be detected before birth through **amniocentesis**, usually done in the second trimester (your notes say after the thirteenth week). A small amount of **amniotic fluid** around the fetus is drawn off and examined for **abnormal chromosomes**.

This allows families and doctors to prepare for the child's needs.

slides.heading: Environment before and after birth
slides.body:
The **prenatal environment** matters greatly. A mother's **high blood pressure**, **diabetes**, **infections**, **drugs or alcohol** can interfere with fetal brain development.

After birth, **low birth weight**, **prematurity**, **accidental falls**, **physical abuse** and early **malnutrition** can damage the brain. Malnutrition's effects can be partly reversed if the child's **diet improves early** (Baroff & Olley, 1999).

slides.question: Which of these is a prenatal risk for intellectual disability?
options: The mother drinking alcohol during pregnancy
The child learning a second language
slides.why: Alcohol and drugs in pregnancy can harm fetal brain development.

slides.heading: Early help in Ibadan
slides.story: Tolu was born with Down syndrome. Her parents enrolled her at 18 months in an early-intervention programme offering speech therapy, play-based learning and parent coaching. By school age she could talk in sentences, dress herself and make friends, and she now attends an inclusive school with support.
slides.takeaway: Early intervention, education and social-skills support help children with intellectual disability develop their potential.

slides.heading: How care has changed
slides.body:
In the past, many children with intellectual disability were placed in **institutions**. Today, especially in Western countries, they are increasingly educated in **community** and **regional** programmes that prepare them for **independent living**.

**Early intervention** offers specialised teaching for infants, toddlers and preschoolers. Help with **social skills** enables easier interaction at school and in the community.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'list some causes of intellectual disability' and short notes on Down syndrome and fragile X. Know 47 chromosomes and trisomy 21, that most Down syndrome is not inherited, and what amniocentesis involves. Trap: saying intellectual disability is a single disease; it is a symptom with many causes.
slides.sampleQuestion: List five causes of intellectual disability.
slides.howToAnswer: Chromosomal disorders (Down syndrome), single-gene defects (fragile X), prenatal exposure to drugs or infections, birth complications, brain trauma, metabolic or nutritional problems (PKU, malnutrition), and psychosocial deprivation or abuse.

points: Intellectual disability is a symptom with many causes.
Down syndrome: extra chromosome 21, usually not inherited.
Fragile X: X-chromosome gene change; PKU: metabolic, preventable by diet.
Amniocentesis detects chromosomal problems before birth.
Prenatal and early-life environment matters; early intervention helps.

questions.explanation: Adolescent diet is not a prenatal factor.

questions.stem: Why is intellectual disability described as a symptom rather than a disease?
options: It results from many different causes
questions.explanation: Many different conditions can produce it.

options: Down syndrome: single gene on X
questions.explanation: PKU is metabolic; Down syndrome is trisomy 21; fragile X is an X-linked gene change.

questions.stem: I. The likelihood of Down syndrome rises with maternal age. II. Down syndrome often involves heart malformations. III. Fragile X is caused by an extra chromosome 21. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are correct. Fragile X is an X-chromosome gene change.

questions.stem: Which change best reflects modern approaches to children with intellectual disability?
options: Early intervention and community-based education preparing for independent living
questions.explanation: Care has shifted from institutions to early intervention and community education.

questions.stem: A child develops intellectual disability after repeated physical abuse causing head injuries. This cause is best classed as:
questions.explanation: Brain injury after birth from abuse is post-natal trauma.

lesson.title: Rett, Asperger's and dyslexia
lesson.hook: A girl develops normally for a year, then gradually loses her speech and starts wringing her hands constantly. A brilliant boy can name every bus route in Lagos but cannot hold a conversation. A bright pupil reads 'was' as 'saw'. Three very different developmental puzzles.

slides.heading: Rett's disorder
slides.body:
**Rett's disorder** differs from autism in its course. Onset is usually between **5 and 48 months**, after **normal early development**. It is rare, about **1 in 10,000**, and occurs **only in girls**.

Head growth **slows**, motor and communication skills **decline**, the child **withdraws socially**, and characteristic **repetitive hand-wringing** movements appear. Most also have intellectual disability. It is **progressive** and caused by **mutations in a gene on the X chromosome**.

slides.heading: Childhood disintegrative disorder
slides.body:
In **childhood disintegrative disorder**, development is **normal until at least age two**. After that, skills already gained start to **slip away** in two or more of these areas: **speech**, **social behaviour** and **movement**. Symptoms resemble autism.

It is more common in **males**. The cause is unknown, probably an abnormality in early nervous-system development. Treatment mirrors autism: **intensive behaviour therapy**, **education** and sometimes **medication**.

slides.heading: Asperger's disorder
slides.body:
Of these conditions, this one shows up **last**: it is often missed until preschool or later. Deficits are **less severe** than in autism, without major language delay. The main problem is **impaired social interaction**, with **repetitive behaviour** and **narrow interests**.

People may avoid eye contact, show little facial expression, and have few friends. It is more common in **males**, and some are **unusually gifted** in particular areas. DSM-5 now includes it within **autism spectrum disorder**.

slides.question: Which developmental disorder occurs only in girls and involves repetitive hand-wringing?
slides.why: Rett's disorder affects girls, with decline after normal early development and hand-wringing movements.

slides.heading: The reliable packer
slides.story: Samuel, diagnosed with Asperger's at ten, finished secondary school with a tutor's help and has packed groceries at a supermarket for over ten years. He is the store's most reliable worker. He greets every customer with the same phrase in the same high tone, looks just past them, and packs bags with exact precision.
slides.takeaway: Asperger's can involve striking social oddities alongside reliability and real strengths.

slides.heading: Learning disorders
slides.body:
**Learning disorders** are **more common** than intellectual disability. They involve **delays in specific cognitive skills**, mainly **language and maths**, not in all mental functioning, and without the severe social problems of pervasive disorders.

Some lagging is normal. A **significant** problem exists when a child is well below the level expected for their **schooling, age and IQ**, typically **more than two years behind**.

steps.title: Reading disorder (dyslexia)
steps.detail: The most common learning disorder; difficulty reading accurately and fluently.

steps.title: Mathematics disorder
steps.detail: Difficulty with number sense, calculation and maths reasoning.

steps.title: Disorder of written expression
steps.detail: Difficulty with spelling, grammar and organising written work.

slides.heading: Dyslexia: causes and help
slides.body:
**Dyslexia** is the most common learning disorder (your notes give about **2%** of school-age children; many estimates are higher). Poor readers are often **late talkers**, **poor spellers**, and have **family histories** of reading difficulty. By age ten, severe reading problems raise the risk of **behaviour problems**.

Theories point to **delayed brain development** or **structural brain differences**. Combining **reading-skills training** with **behavioural** methods that keep the child motivated works for many.

slides.question: The three main types of learning disorder are:
options: Reading disorder, mathematics disorder and disorder of written expression
slides.why: Learning disorders affect reading, maths and written expression.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'mention the three main types of learning disorders' and short notes on Rett's, childhood disintegrative and Asperger's disorders. Key distinctions: Rett's only girls; CDD normal until at least 2 then regression; Asperger's latest onset, milder. Trap: thinking learning disorders mean low overall intelligence; they are specific delays.
slides.sampleQuestion: Which developmental disorder has the latest onset and the least severe deficits? (a) autism (b) Rett's disorder (c) Asperger's disorder (d) childhood disintegrative disorder
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (c). Describe its social impairment, narrow interests and occasional special gifts, and note DSM-5 now places it within the autism spectrum.

points: Rett's: girls only, decline after normal start, hand-wringing, X-linked gene.
Childhood disintegrative disorder: normal to 2+, then loss of skills.
Asperger's: latest onset, milder, social impairment, narrow interests.
Learning disorders: specific delays, often more than two years behind.
Reading, maths and written expression; dyslexia is most common.

questions.explanation: Skill training combined with motivation-focused behaviour therapy helps many.

questions.stem: Why does DSM-5 group autism, Asperger's and childhood disintegrative disorder together?
options: They are all caused by Down syndrome

questions.explanation: They are seen as points on one autism spectrum.
